blocks.content: OOP is powerful but it is not always the right tool. Forcing everything into classes and objects when the problem doesn't call for it creates unnecessary complexity, harder-to-read code, and bugs that wouldn't exist otherwise.
1. The Trap most developers fall into
blocks.text: 1. The Trap most developers fall into

blocks.content: When you learn OOP well, everything starts to look like a candidate for a class. A utility function becomes a UtilityManager.
A config file becomes a ConfigurationService. A simple data record becomes an object with a dozen methods it doesn't need.
This is sometimes called overengineering and it's one of the most common mistakes in software design.
The question is never "can I use OOP here?" the answer to that is almost always yes. The question is "does OOP make this simpler or more complex?"

THE RULE OF THUMB: If adding a class requires more explanation than the problem itself, you don't need the class. Complexity you introduce must earn its keep by making the overall system cleaner not just more "structured-looking."
2. The 6 situations where OOP hurts more than it helps
blocks.text: 2. The 6 situations where OOP hurts more than it helps

blocks.content: OOP is a powerful tool but like every tool in software engineering, using it everywhere often creates more complexity than clarity.
1. Simple data transformations and pipelines
blocks.text: 1. Simple data transformations and pipelines

blocks.content: When all you're doing is taking some data in, transforming it, and sending it out there are no entities, no shared state, no identity. A class would just be a wrapper around one or two functions that don't belong together.

["OOP UNNECESSARY CLASS
"]
A TaxCalculator class with one method that takes a number and returns a number. You never store state. You never extend it. The class adds zero value.

["BETTER PURE FUNCTION
"]
Just write calculateTax(amount, rate). One line, instantly testable, no instantiation, no boilerplate, no confusion about which instance to use.
2: Scripts and one-off automation tasks

A script that runs once, does a job, and exits doesn't need a class hierarchy. Renaming 500 files, migrating a database, generating a report — these are sequential steps, not entities with state and behaviour. OOP adds ceremony without benefit.
THE TELL: If your class is instantiated exactly once, used immediately, and never referenced again it's a function wearing a costume. Remove the class, keep the logic.
3. Highly concurrent and parallel systems

OOP objects hold mutable state. When multiple threads access and modify that state simultaneously, you get race conditions, deadlocks, and bugs that only appear on production under load the worst kind.
Functional approaches that avoid shared mutable state are dramatically safer in concurrent systems. Immutable data can be read by 1000 threads simultaneously without any locking.

["OOP RISK
"]
Two threads call order.updateStatus()simultaneously. Without careful locking, both read the old status, both write, and one write is silently lost.

["FUNCTIONAL SAFETY
"]
Instead of mutating the order, return a new order with the updated status. Neither thread touches shared memory no race, no lock needed.
4. Data-heavy ML and scientific computing

Machine learning pipelines, signal processing, numerical computations these are overwhelmingly about applying mathematical transformations to arrays of numbers. The "entities" are matrices and tensors, not objects with rich behaviour.
Libraries like NumPy, Pandas, and TensorFlow are designed around functional-style operations precisely because that's what the problem domain calls for.
Wrapping these in OOP abstractions usually just gets in the way.

REAL WORLD EXAMPLE

A Python ML pipeline: load data → normalise → train → evaluate. These are transformations, not objects. The most readable version is a sequence of function calls not a DataLoader, Normaliser, Trainer class hierarchy.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 5. Premature abstraction, designing for imaginary future requirements

OOP encourages thinking about extension points and polymorphism. That's valuable when you actually need them. The trap is building elaborate class hierarchies for requirements you don't have yet and may never have.

You build a NotificationStrategy interface, three implementations, a factory, and an abstract base class for a system that currently sends exactly one type of email. That's six files for one sendEmail() call.

["THE IMAGINARY EXTENSIBILITY TRAP
"]
"We might need to support SMS someday." So you build the entire Strategy pattern now. Someday doesn't come. The code rotts and confuses every new engineer who reads it.

["THE RIGHT APPROACH
"]
Build for what you need now. Refactor when the requirement actually arrives. Clean, simple code is far easier to extend later than over-abstracted code added prematurely.

YAGNI: YOU AIN'T GONNA NEED IT: One of the most important principles in software. Don't add complexity for requirements you don't have. The cost of wrong abstractions is higher than the cost of refactoring when the time comes.
6. Configuration and plain data records

A config object database URL, API keys, port numbers is just data. It doesn't have behaviour, it doesn't have identity, it doesn't change over time. Wrapping it in a class with getters and setters adds lines of code without adding clarity.

Before reaching for a class, run through this quick check.

The bottom line

OOP shines when your problem has real-world entities with identity, state, and behaviour orders, users, payments, drivers. It struggles when the problem is just a sequence of transformations, a config record, or a one-time script.

["USE OOP WHEN
"]
The problem has entities with identity and changing state. Multiple parts of the codebase need to interact with the same concept. The system will grow and be maintained by a team.

["SKIP OOP WHEN
"]
You're transforming data without storing state. The logic runs once and exits. You're in a concurrent system where shared mutable state is dangerous. The abstraction would outlive its usefulness.

THE EXPERT INSTINCT: Senior engineers default to the simplest thing that works. They reach for a class when the problem genuinely calls for one not because they know OOP, but because they know when not to use it. That discernment is what separates a good engineer from a great one.
